vignette:
Margot

Margot Kovács was seventy-six when she finally made the appointment with a trauma therapist, though she had been carrying the weight of her childhood for more than sixty years. She had built a life of impressive surfaces—a career as a city council member spanning three decades, a reputation for unflinching advocacy on behalf of vulnerable populations, a divorce behind her that she had managed with practical efficiency. Yet in recent months, something had begun to unravel that all her competence and control could not repair.

The original wound was a simple, terrible fact: her father had beaten her mother in their Budapest apartment when Margot was eight years old. She did not have a clear image of the event itself—the memory had a quality of being pushed away, as if her younger self had learned to interrupt the full recall before it could crystallize into something unbearable. What remained instead was the emotional core, intact and volatile: the sound of her mother's cry, the helplessness, the terror that someone she loved was being destroyed and she was powerless to stop it. That feeling, raw and unmediated, would arrive without warning—in a doctor's office, in a conversation with a colleague, in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday—with an intensity that made the present moment feel thin and unreal by comparison.

Three months ago, Margot had undergone a routine colonoscopy. The procedure itself was unremarkable, but in the moments before sedation, lying on the table in the hospital gown, she had felt the full emotional weight of that childhood afternoon descend on her without any accompanying image. Her heart had raced. She had felt trapped. The technician's hand on her arm—meant to be reassuring—had triggered a cascade of panic that she could not explain to anyone present. She had asked the doctor to stop the procedure. She had not completed it.

Since then, she had begun to avoid medical appointments. She had cancelled her annual physical. She had postponed a dental cleaning. What frightened her most was not the procedures themselves but the vulnerability, the loss of control, the way her body seemed to become a conduit for emotions that belonged to a different time entirely. She had come to believe that if she could simply avoid those situations—the examining rooms, the moments of helplessness—she could keep herself safe from whatever was waiting to overwhelm her.

But avoidance had consequences that spread beyond the medical sphere. When her younger sister had mentioned, almost casually, that their father had been suffering from dementia in his final years, Margot had felt the old emotion surge again—not sadness or forgiveness, but that same raw terror and rage. She had ended the conversation abruptly and had not spoken to her sister since. Comments about family, even oblique ones, had become dangerous. She had withdrawn from her extended family's holiday gatherings, offering work as an excuse.

Worse, she had begun to see her father everywhere. Last month, at a city council meeting, a constituent had reminded her of him—the same heavy build, the same way of speaking with absolute certainty. She had found herself unable to concentrate for the remainder of the session. The man's face had stayed with her, vivid and immediate in a way that made her current surroundings feel distant and false. Her memories of the beating itself were fragmented, but her memory of him—the offender—had become crystalline, more present to her than the actual faces of people she saw every day.

It was her chief of staff who had finally insisted she seek help. Margot had missed a critical vote due to a cancelled medical appointment, and her increasing isolation had begun to affect her work. She sat in the therapist's office now, composed and articulate as always, but aware that something essential in her was coming undone—that the careful architecture she had built to contain her past was no longer holding.
